entries.title: 'Coalition of the Willing' meets in Berlin: In an era of waning support, Europe remains committed to Ukraine
entries.summary: The "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine is gathering in Berlin. One of the key issues under discussion is whether Europe will be able to play a role in future negotiations over the country's future.
entries.content:
Germany

'Coalition of the Willing' meets in Berlin over Ukraine's future

November 18, 2026

The "Coalition of the Willing" supporting Ukraine is gathering in Berlin. One of the key issues under discussion is whether Europe will be able to play a role in future negotiations over the country's future.

Once again, Berlin is rolling out the red carpet, and once again the focus is on Ukraine: around 20 heads of state and government, primarily from across Europe, are set to gather in the German capital on Thursday (November 19). They will discuss the future of the Eastern European country that has been under attack from Russia since February 2022 and is now facing yet another harsh winter.

Extensive security measures have already been announced for Berlin's government district, pointing to the presence of high-ranking participants. It remains unclear whether Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy will be among them. What does appear certain, however, is the attendance of chief US negotiators Steve Witkoff and Jared Kushner, according to several media outlets.

The "Coalition of the Willing" is a group of 36 countries determined not to be deterred from supporting the nation under attack. Unlike other international forums, the group is focused not only on how to support Ukraine militarily and financially in the here and now.

Led by Germany, France, and the United Kingdom, the coalition is also prepared, in principle, to help monitor a possible ceasefire within Ukraine itself and to contribute to the complex security guarantees the country would then require, should such a scenario come to pass. The effort dates back to March 2025, when the countries involved first met in London. Now they are gathering in Berlin.

But what can the coalition realistically achieve? Stefan Meister of the German Council on Foreign Relations (DGAP) is not overly optimistic. In an interview with DW, he said: "The fundamental problem is that Europe has yet to put forward a proposal. There is no plan outlining what security guarantees Europe would offer, what troops it would be prepared to deploy, what measures it could provide to safeguard a ceasefire, or where it would be willing to make compromises."

Merz: 'Germany has a seat at the table'

Nevertheless, the meeting comes at a moment when some observers believe there may finally be movement toward ending the war. During talks in Abu Dhabi in the United Arab Emirates a few days ago, Russia, Ukraine, and the US managed to agree only on a prisoner exchange. It was a modest step forward.

Further talks are planned, and it has been a long time since the prospects appeared as favorable as they do now for Europe to secure a role in future decisions on war and peace in Ukraine.

It has repeatedly been argued, both by US officials and by those in power in Russia, that Europe does not speak with a single voice.

Unsurprisingly, this has sparked a debate among EU heads of state and government over who, exactly, could represent Europe in such talks. Could it be German Chancellor Friedrich Merz of the center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU)? After the EU summit in Dublin, Ireland, on Friday, he said: "For the first time, concrete peace talks are expected to take place in the coming weeks with Europe represented. Germany has a seat at the table, that is absolutely clear."

Europe has yet to speak with one voice

But what exactly did that mean? That Germany alone would speak for all of Europe? Hardly. As was also made clear in Berlin on Monday, Europe would be represented by the E3 countries, namely Germany, France, and the non-EU member United Kingdom, joined by Poland and Italy. Official EU representatives, including European Council President António Costa, would also take part.

Stefan Meister of the DGAP believes the debate says a great deal about the pressures Europe itself is under: "Europe's positioning has more to do with domestic political considerations than with developments in the negotiations. Everyone needs to show that they are participating in the talks in some way. Elections will be held next year in France and Poland, and it is still unclear whether French support for Ukraine will continue in its current form after that."

German Deputy Government Spokesperson Sebastian Hille, meanwhile, sought to downplay the debate on Monday over a possible role for Friedrich Merz as chief negotiator. At the federal government's regular press briefing, he said: "This is not about discussing individuals. What matters is that Putin finally understands that he must come to the negotiating table so that we have a chance of achieving peace in the first place."

German government spokesperson: Europe now needs stamina

US negotiator Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, struck a rather different tone last week. Speaking in Abu Dhabi, he said: "If Europe could identify one person to speak on their behalf, that would be a bigger achievement than getting the Russians to include them in the negotiations."

Government spokesperson Hille responded on Monday: "Europe's strength lies precisely in the unity and cohesion of many countries. We should not allow ourselves to be drawn into debates that others want to frame around this question." Hille emphasized that the situation remained unchanged: peace in Ukraine could only be achieved step by step. Europe, too, would need stamina, perseverance, and a willingness to undertake the painstaking work required to bring it about.

Declining support for Ukraine in German polls

European supporters of Ukraine are also under pressure as public opinion on the issue is shifting, including in Germany. While a broad majority favored helping defend the country in the immediate aftermath of Russia's invasion in the spring of 2022, support has since fallen markedly.

According to the latest ARD DeutschlandTrend survey on the issue, conducted in September 2026, 52% of eligible voters still support weapons deliveries to Ukraine, while 42% believe such support has gone too far. That is the highest level of opposition recorded since the start of the war.

A further study conducted for public broadcaster WDR in November 2026 found that support for Ukraine has become a more polarizing issue in Germany than immigration. According to the survey, 54% of respondents favor continued support for Ukraine, while just under 29% would prefer a rapprochement with Russia, despite its war of aggression against Ukraine.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Has the 'Parthenon puzzle' been solved? The long quest to reassemble lost eastern pediment
entries.summary: The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.
entries.content:
November 18, 2026

The depiction of the birth of the goddess Athena above the Parthenon's entrance is considered a masterpiece of ancient art. Now, a German research team has pieced together all the surviving fragments.

The 2,500-year-old Parthenon is ancient Greece's most important temple and is regarded as one of the greatest masterpieces of the High Classical period of Greek art.

Dedicated to Athena, the city's patron goddess, it towers over Athens from its position on the Acropolis — a powerful symbol of the city's importance.

The Parthenon had a lasting influence on Western ideas of humanity and art. The sculptures adorning its pediments, created under the direction of the legendary sculptor Phidias, are considered unparalleled examples of proportion and grace. They have influenced artists from ancient Rome through Neoclassicism to the modern era.

'Very confident we've solved the mystery'

The east pediment above the temple entrance depicted the birth of the goddess Athena from the head of her father Zeus, surrounded by the Olympian gods. A total of 39 figures adorned the roughly 29-meter-long work of art. At its center stood a colossal Zeus figure, measuring 3.8 meters in height.

For centuries, scholars have puzzled over exactly what the arrangement looked like, as the pediment was destroyed during the Christianization of Greece.

But now there has been a breakthrough.

After decades of painstaking detective work and with the help of modern technology, archaeologist Vinzenz Brinkmann and his team have managed to piece together all the surviving fragments of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann heads the Antiquities and Asia department at Frankfurt's Liebieghaus sculpture collection. "We're very, very confident that we've solved the mystery," he told DW.

The results are now on display in an exhibition at the Liebieghaus titled "Athena, the Stage is Yours: The Parthenon Puzzle."

Only around 20% of the original marble sculpture's volume is known to have survived. The fragments are scattered across various European museums, with most located in Athens. The British Museum also holds numerous pieces.

Brinkmann and his wife, Ulrike Koch-Brinkmann, have spent more than 40 years working on this ancient puzzle, with so many of its pieces missing.

And they were far from the first to attempt it: "Already in the 19th century, many scholars studied the subject and developed well-founded theories based on their deep knowledge of ancient sources," Brinkmann explains.

In 1910, a study documenting the many fragments held by the British Museum was published. The research team was able to build on that earlier work, but progress remained slow for years.

Then, in 2014, a visit to the Hermitage Museum in St. Petersburg provided Brinkmann with a crucial clue. There, he encountered a Roman sarcophagus featuring a relief of Athena's birth. "That's when it suddenly clicked: They're all there!"

Nine such sarcophagi are known to exist, almost all of them in Rome. Each depicts a different section of the Parthenon's east pediment.

Brinkmann emphasizes that other scholars had already noticed this connection in the 19th century. "But we really seized on the idea and never let go."

A handy tool: the iPhone

The researchers also benefited from 21st-century technology: 3D scanners and printers. Brinkmann and his team visited numerous destinations to examine around 60 original fragments at different locations — traveling light. An iPhone was all they needed to scan the pieces.

Digitally fitting the fragments together led to another important discovery. "We know these figures we're putting together!" Brinkmann recalls thinking at the time.

The Romans had repeatedly made individual copies of all the sculptures from the pediment. "These copies matched the fragments perfectly. Suddenly, we found ourselves surrounded by old acquaintances we had never suspected had come from the pediment." This finally enabled the researchers to reconstruct all the figures and their original arrangement.

Using a 3D printer, the team created a 4-meter-long model at a scale of 1:7.7. For the exhibition, they also produced life-size 3D prints of the most important fragments and mounted them on panels depicting the complete figures at their original size. An animation brings the reconstructed composition to life, digitally assembling the fragments to reveal how the east pediment once looked.

Alongside works from the Liebieghaus collection, the exhibition features loans from other institutions, including the Vatican Museums and the Louvre. Objects from the Acropolis Museum in Athens had originally been expected as well. But Greece withdrew its participation after learning that the British Museum was also planning to lend fragments to the Frankfurt exhibition. The Liebieghaus ultimately decided to forgo the British-owned fragments, too.

The dispute between Greece and Britain over the Parthenon sculptures

There is a reason for this controversy. Britain holds a substantial portion of the Parthenon frieze as well as fragments from both pediments.

Greek authorities have been campaigning for their return for decades.

In Britain, the 56 sections of the frieze are known as the "Elgin Marbles," named after Lord Elgin, the British ambassador to the Ottoman Empire in Constantinople.

In the early 19th century, Elgin had sculptures removed from the exterior of the Parthenon on the Acropolis in Athens. They were taken to Britain with the consent of the Ottoman Empire, which ruled Greece at the time.

Britain maintains that the sculptures were legally acquired.

Greece, however, considers them stolen.

For years, the dispute remained deadlocked. Since the Labour Party came to power in Britain, there has been some movement toward resolving it. But apparently not enough to persuade Greece to lend artworks to an exhibition in which the British Museum might also participate.

The exhibition "Athena, the Stage is Yours. The Parthenon Puzzle" runs through July 25, 2027, at the Liebieghaus in Frankfurt.

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: India: Online censorship grows after 'Cockroach' protests
entries.summary: Since anti-government Cockroach protests erupted, journalists and creators say their content is increasingly being restricted on social media in India.
entries.content:
India

India: Online censorship grows after 'Cockroach' protests

November 18, 2026

Since anti-government Cockroach protests erupted, journalists and creators say their content is increasingly being restricted on social media in India.

A video showing a young girl crying as she spoke about alleged police brutality during the youth-led Cockroach Janata Party (CJP) protests in July. A video examining the Hindu nationalist Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh's (RSS) contribution to the rise of India's ruling Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP). A satirical cartoon criticizing Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government.

These are among the examples of content that have recently been restricted on social media in India.

A pattern of restrictions

Content creator CitySavitri describes herself as a "nobody" in the world of social media. She had started making videos just two months ago and had around 600 followers on Instagram.

Yet a video looking at the RSS's role in the BJP's 2014 election victory was restricted in India within an hour of being posted. It was the first of three videos she posted that faced restrictions.

The experience made her feel that "anti-government commentary" was being monitored and curtailed.

"It is very plain and simple to understand," the content creator told DW.

Independent journalist Sadhika Tiwari was covering the CJP protest in New Delhi on July 20, when police used batons and tear gas against demonstrators.

Tiwari's video of a frightened young girl crying and speaking about police brutality garnered around 10 million views within hours, she said, before it was restricted in India.

Political cartoonist Satish Acharya has also faced repeated restrictions, with Instagram blocking his profile twice recently.

'Suppressing independent journalism'

In May 2025, during the conflict between India and Pakistan, independent digital news outlet Maktoob Media's X account was withheld in India while it was reporting on the escalating crisis, its founder and editor Aslah Kayyalakkath told DW.

"We received no official notice or email from either the government or X. It was our readers who first alerted us to the blocking," he said.

Maktoob Media said it contacted Indian officials and X but received no response. Access to the account was restored a few days later, again without an explanation.

Kayyalakkath said Maktoob's content from the July protest also faced restrictions. "Suppressing independent journalism undermines transparency, accountability and democratic values," he said.

Several of the content creators and journalists interviewed by DW said they received no prior notification or explanation for the restrictions.

Some users were not sure if their content had been blocked at the government's request or proactively by the social media platforms.

When asked for comment, Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, pointed DW to a website statement noting users can appeal content and account restrictions.

How does the system work?

At the heart of the debate are India's IT Rules, 2021, amended in February 2026. Section 79 of India's IT Act protects social media platforms and other intermediaries from liability for content posted by third parties, provided they meet certain legal conditions.

One such requirement, introduced through the February 2026 amendments, is to remove or disable access to specified unlawful content within three hours of receiving a valid court order or a reasoned government notice. The previous deadline was 36 hours.

Failure to comply can result in intermediaries losing their liability protection.

The government's Sahyog portal, which coordinates takedown requests between law enforcement, platforms and telecom providers, has faced criticism over the pace at which notices are issued.

Meta said it uses automated tools and technologies to detect and review content that may violate its community standards. It also automatically restricts access to certain types of content in India to comply with legal requirements under the IT rules.

Pranesh Prakash, a technology law and policy adviser, said the amended rules allow authorized police officials to notify intermediaries about content they consider unlawful without necessarily filing a formal complaint or initiating other legal proceedings.

"This has led to the worst period of social media censorship that India has ever seen, with digital news media accounts being blocked, cartoonists' accounts being blocked, and even mere discussions of an opposition leader's memoirs being blocked," he said. "Clearly, none of these disclosed any 'unlawful acts.'"

Prakash also raised concerns about the lack of public information on government requests to remove content, saying this made it difficult to assess the scale of restrictions.

A flaw in the system

The Software Freedom Law Center, India (SFLC.in), a digital rights organization, said the growing reliance on automated takedowns raised serious concerns about transparency, accountability and due process.

"There is little transparency about the processes through which content is identified, flagged and restricted, or whether there is any meaningful human oversight before a takedown is implemented," SFLC.in told DW.

The organization also tested X's verification process by submitting a takedown request against one of its own posts using a fake email address. X registered the request, raising questions about how it verified the identity and authority of those submitting requests.

After SFLC.in alerted the company, X introduced email verification codes for people submitting takedown requests.

"A channel that lets anyone pose as a law enforcement official can be misused to silence lawful speech," SFLC.in said.

X did not respond to DW's request for a comment.

Government says no censorship

The Indian government denies that it is censoring online content.

While the ministry did not respond to DW's latest request for a comment, in an email response to DW in August, Vinod Kumar, chief of media and communications at the Information Technology Ministry, said Instagram posts by students and protesters following the July CJP protests "are not being taken down as alleged."

"Media enjoys freedom in India. The Government does not censor online content," Kumar said, adding that the government only acts against "objectionable content."

Under the Indian IT rules, "unlawful content" generally refers to material which could threaten India's sovereignty and integrity, disturb public order, incite violence, or constitute defamation.

However, social media influencers such as university professor Madri Kakoti, alias Dr. Medusa, continue to report restrictions. Kakoti's Instagram account was restricted in India on November 16 without notice, she said, along with that of satirist Shamita Yadav.

The price of free speech

Rights groups including Human Rights Watch have warned that expanding content restrictions could chill free expression and encourage self-censorship among journalists, creators and ordinary users. 

Acharya, however, said he would continue his work.

"The Indian Constitution gives me the right to draw political cartoons," he said. "It's totally democratic to question and criticize the government in India."

For Tiwari, the issue goes beyond the reach of a single video. It is also about preserving a record of what happened, after the Delhi Police denied allegations of using excessive force during the July 20 protest in front of the Supreme Court.

"We have seen several other videos now, and it's well established why that girl was crying, and that the Delhi Police used force and lied about it," she said.

"Still, I want that video back up because it needs to stay for posterity. I think that's the larger idea: they want to take this stuff down so it fades from memory, allowing them to categorically deny it later when we have little left to show for what happened."

entries.title: ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What to know
entries.summary: The ICJ is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country's Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.
entries.content:
Myanmar

ICJ to rule on Rohingya genocide case against Myanmar: What to know

November 18, 2026

The ICJ is set to decide whether Myanmar's military operations in Rakhine State a decade ago were carried out with the intent to destroy the country's Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) will deliver on Thursday its long-awaited judgment in The Gambia's landmark genocide case against Myanmar, seven years after the case was lodged in The Hague.  

The Gambia filed the case with the United Nations' top court in November 2019, formally accusing the Southeast Asian nation of breaking its obligations under the 1948 UN Genocide Convention.

In documents and hearings, The Gambia has alleged that Myanmar waged a deliberate campaign of arson, rape and murder in Rakhine State from 2016 to 2017, intending to wipe out the area's ethnic Rohingya minority, in whole or in part.

A UN fact-finding mission later concluded that some 10,000 people likely died in the pogroms. Another 700,000 Rohingya fled the country to neighboring Bangladesh, where most of them still live today in the world's largest refugee settlement.

Even before 2016, the predominantly Muslim Rohingya had been subjected to decades of persecution by the Buddhist-majority country's government, with many forced into resettlement camps and most denied citizenship.

A number of cases over Myanmar's treatment of the Rohingya have been filed in courts around the world. The ICJ will be the first to issue a ruling.

"The Rohingya people have been waiting for justice for decades for the atrocities and crimes committed against [us]. There were no venues available in [Myanmar]…. International venues were the only hope," said Aung Kyaw Moe, a prominent Rohingya activist whose family was forced to flee the country during the pogroms.

"We've come over many years to a situation where a judgment will be delivered, and the expectation from the Rohingya community is very high," he said.

Journey to judgment day

A month after The Gambia lodged its case with the ICJ in 2019, Nobel laureate Aung San Suu Kyi, Myanmar's de facto civilian leader at the time, traveled to The Hague to contest the allegations, calling them "incomplete and incorrect."

The move tarnished her international reputation as a human rights icon. Many human rights advocates criticized her for defending the very military that had persecuted her for most of her life.

In 2020, ahead of a final judgment, the ICJ issued emergency "provisional measures" ordering Myanmar to take all steps "within its power" to prevent acts of genocide against the Rohingya, an order rights groups say it has blatantly ignored.

Myanmar's military went on to oust the country's democratically elected government the following year, placing Aung San Suu Kyi under arrest and setting off a bloody civil war that continues to rage.

Myanmar also challenged both the court's jurisdiction over the alleged crimes and The Gambia's right to lodge the case, both of which the ICJ rejected in 2022.

The ICJ then held 14 days of hearings this January for Myanmar and The Gambia to make their arguments before the panel. While Myanmar called one witness, The Gambia called three, as well as an expert.

A question of intent

As The Gambia has accused Myanmar of breaking several articles of the Genocide Convention, Thursday's judgment could be "fairly complicated," said Melanie O'Brien, a professor of international law at the University of Western Australia and past president of the International Association of Genocide Scholars.

The convention outlines that states have a duty to prevent and punish genocide and to establish effective penalties for those found responsible. The ICJ could rule in Myanmar's favor on some of these provisions and against it on others.

"So, there's quite a lot of layers here. They'll be looking at all of those issues, along with, of course, delving into the facts of the case and the individual crimes of genocide and whether or not Myanmar committed those individual crimes with the intent to destroy the Rohingya," O'Brien said.

Proving Myanmar's intent behind the alleged atrocities is the key question the ICJ is grappling with.

Myanmar argues that its actions were strictly part of a legitimate counterinsurgency and counterterrorism operation, and that those actions could not at the same time be judged as acts of genocide.

Days before the Myanmar military launched its heaviest operations in Rakhine, in August 2017, the Arakan Rohingya Salvation Army, an armed group based in the state, staged a coordinated attack on more than 30 police posts, killing several officers.

Either-or, maybe both

The Gambia argues that Myanmar's actions can qualify as both counterinsurgency and genocide at the same time. It also argues that the sexual violence and killing of children that accompanied the operations are proof that genocide was part of the goal.

"It directly undermines Myanmar's argument that this was a legitimate counterterrorism operation," said Michael Becker, an associate professor of international human rights law at Trinity College Dublin and a former associate legal officer at the ICJ.

"Because evidence of those types of atrocities are very hard to square with the idea that this had some other purpose beyond terrorizing the Rohingya population and indeed taking actions to try to destroy them," he said.

O'Brien and Becker said The Gambia's case against Myanmar is a chance for the ICJ to clarify how it weighs such circumstantial or indirect evidence when judging whether genocide has taken place.

Because investigators were denied access to Rakhine State, they had to rely on interviews with victims and witnesses who had fled Myanmar and on reports by the UN and other groups.

"And how the court deals with that, whether the ICJ accepts or rejects The Gambia's view or Myanmar's view of genocidal intent and how you prove it, this will have major repercussions for other cases," said Becker.

Justice denied vs. delayed

The ICJ is grappling with some of the same questions in cases between the Democratic Republic of Congo and Rwanda, Ukraine and Russia, and South Africa and Israel.

"I'm sure that the parties in the other cases will pick up on what the court rules in this case and add it to their own cases," said O'Brien.

"And even though this case will only be binding on The Gambia and Myanmar, the court itself may also refer to its own law in their future cases," she added.

The ICJ's judgment may have some effect on not only other cases but other courts as well.

The International Criminal Court — which, unlike the ICJ, tries individuals and not states — is considering an arrest warrant request for Myanmar coup leader Min Aung Hlaing in a trial on alleged crimes against humanity committed against the Rohingya. Becker and O'Brien say a finding of genocide by the ICJ could bolster the case for granting the warrant.

What a finding of genocide would actually do for the Rohingya is another key question.

Enforcing any reparations or restitution the court may order would rest with the UN Security Council. But with China and Russia, both allies of Min Aung Hlaing's regime, holding veto power on the council, there are serious doubts about whether it would act on any court order on Myanmar.

Aung Kyaw Moe remains hopeful that the Rohingya will one day receive justice.

"Despite these challenges, there are a lot of hopes that we can [move] toward the betterment of the Rohingya people, including compensation, reparations, transitional justice in the domestic setting in the long term," he said.

entries.title: Axes and cutlasses: Violence on Nigeria's election campaign trail
entries.summary: As Nigeria's January 2027 elections approach, political violence and thuggery at campaign rallies and town hall meetings raise concerns about voter safety.
entries.content:
Nigeria

Axes and cutlasses: Violence on Nigeria's election campaign trail

November 18, 2026

As Nigeria's January 2027 elections approach, political violence and thuggery at campaign rallies and town hall meetings raise concerns about voter safety.

Samuel Adebanjo had gone to the Oregun area of Lagos, the economic heartbeat of Nigeria, to cover a town hall meeting organized by the opposition party, the National Democratic Congress (NDC). But what was supposed to be a routine reporting assignment took a violent turn when a group of armed men stormed the venue and disrupted the gathering.

"I was at the entrance, taking photos of people entering the hall when some buses drove in and I heard a loud bang," Samuel recalled. Before he could process what was happening, the men began chasing supporters of the party with axes, cutlasses, and wooden planks, forcing many to flee for safety.

Adebanjo ran towards the parking lot, hoping to find somewhere to hide. But some of the attackers spotted him and gave chase. The journalist with the local newspaper, The Cable, was surrounded by five men who started hitting him to make him let go of his camera. Despite wearing a press jacket, they accused him of being the party's cameraman. "They wanted to collect the camera. I was struggling with them because I didn't want them to take it away. In the process, my middle finger was broken," he said.

During the struggle, one of the thugs raised his axe and struck it towards his wrist. "I used my hand to guard it. I was expecting blood. I never knew it landed on my wristwatch, and that's when it hit me that they're not joking, and that I had to let go of my equipment."

He was left in agonizing pain. By the time the violence subsided and he was taken to the hospital, he had sustained a broken middle finger and internal injuries around his ribs. The attack also left several other people injured and properties, including vehicles belonging to supporters of the party, destroyed.

As the January 16, 2027 general election inches closer, incidents like this are becoming increasingly common, as incumbent Bola Tinubu battles for re-election on a ticket that revolves around combating insecurity and resolving the country's biting economic crisis.

Election-related violence on the rise

Adebanjo's experience is not an isolated incident. According to the National Peace Committee, 109 breaches of the National Peace Accord have been recorded across the country's 26 states and the federal capital, Abuja.

Between August 19, when the campaign kicked off in the West African country, and October 27, political violence and thuggery, as well as misinformation and disinformation, top the violations, accounting for 33 and 29 incidents respectively.

Campaign rallies, town hall meetings and other political events organized by parties have been marred by violence, threats and intimidation, prompting analysts to caution that rising violence could taint the credibility of the elections and discourage voter participation.

On November 15, a group of men attacked the campaign convoy of former Kano state governor and National Democratic Congress vice-presidential candidate Rabiu Kwankwaso during a visit to the Bichi area of Kano. Similar incidents were recorded in both Sokoto and Kebbi when former Vice President Atiku Abubakar took his campaign to the northwestern states.

Civil society groups, including Amnesty International, have condemned the spate of election-related violence and intimidation across the country, urging security agencies to bring perpetrators to book. President Tinubu has also condemned the rising incidents of violence at political events, warning that intimidation and political thuggery capable of disrupting public order would not be tolerated.

Nigeria's history of electoral violence

Political violence is not new to Nigeria; nearly all of the country's elections have been tainted by violence and intimidation, including the deadly post-election violence that followed the 2011 elections, where at least 800 people were killed over days of rioting in states across northern Nigeria.

Raheem Mutiu, a Nigerian researcher at Armed Conflict Location & Event Data (ACLED), a global organization that collects data on conflicts and political violence worldwide, told DW that the pattern ahead of the coming polls is shaping up to show "political groups more agitated and determined to win elections by all means."

Mutiu described the spate of violence since the campaign was flagged off as mind-boggling. "Within the period of two months, we have recorded over 30 politically linked attacks with 10 fatalities. But what this one points to is that politically linked attacks have become more frequent and geographically widespread ahead of the January 2027 general election," he said.

The country's multiparty politics has entrenched a winner-takes-all system that fuels fierce competition among parties and, at times, a willingness to resort to violence. There's also a growing intolerance for opposition among party supporters, although perpetrators are difficult to identify because they often act anonymously and as proxies for the interests they support.

"What we have seen again is that supporters across the political spectrum are involved in the attacks, but intensity of their violence and engagement largely depends on their local stronghold and territorial dominance," Mutiu added.

The high cost of violence

A voter choosing under threat is not choosing freely, Dengiyefa Angalapu, a researcher at the Abuja-based Center for Democracy and Development, told DW. He noted that apart from the physical attacks, the spread of fake news and hate speech narratives, which form part of the non-physical breaches of the peace accord, "can deceive voters and undermine trust in genuine information."

Angalapu stressed that the growing threat of electoral violence could further undermine voter participation in a country already struggling with low turnout. More than 103 million Nigerians are registered to vote in the 2027 general elections, according to the country's electoral authority.

However, the country has consistently recorded low voter participation, with the 2023 general elections witnessing the lowest turnout since Nigeria's return to democratic rule in 1999. Only 27% of the nearly 94 million registered voters cast their ballots.

 "Intimidation adds another pressure: someone who fears punishment for their political preference may avoid meetings or withdraw from politics altogether," Angalapu added.

Adebanjo is still recovering from his injuries. The attack has left him with a bigger question about safety ahead of the polls: "If this could happen to me, a journalist, how much more to the citizens? I am not sure, at this stage, people will even come out to vote."

entries.title: Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?
entries.summary: El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. But experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable or compatible with human rights.
entries.content:
Latin America

Latin America's mega-prisons: Can El Salvador's model work?

November 18, 2026

El Salvador's mega-prison has become a model for governments across Latin America seeking to combat organized crime. But experts question whether the approach is effective, sustainable or compatible with human rights.

Around 15,000 inmates and a capacity of up to 40,000, prison sentences of up to 1,000 years, strict security measures and an extreme isolation regime. Staged images show inmates with shaved heads and tattoos being subdued by heavily armed guards.

These are just some of the facts circulating about El Salvador's Terrorism Confinement Center (CECOT), a symbol of President Nayib Bukele's security policy and a possible model for other Latin American countries seeking to combat organized crime.

More than a dozen governments in the region have proposed building similar "mega-prisons," although most would have a far smaller capacity. A range of experts consulted by DW question the effectiveness and sustainability of these initiatives.

What is a mega-prison?

De facto mega-prisons — that is, overcrowded prisons with excessive inmate populations — existed in Latin America long before Bukele, says criminologist Jose Luis Perez Guadalupe, former president of the National Penitentiary Institute and former interior minister in Peru. Lurigancho Prison in Lima, for example, designed to hold 3,000 inmates, has housed nearly 11,000 for decades.

But ever since CECOT was launched in 2023, the concept of a "mega-prison" has been primarily linked to maximum-security facilities. For Olga Espinoza, an academic specializing in prison systems at the School of Government of the University of Chile, this association is problematic because it implies that the entire prison population requires "extremely severe" punishment.

High costs and a questionable track record

According to Espinoza, placing the entire prison population in maximum-security facilities would amount to inefficient and extremely costly "over-intervention." These facilities require substantial investments in infrastructure, technology, specialized staff, anti-corruption measures and social reintegration programs.

It would also be ineffective because "international evidence indicates that when people with different profiles are placed in the same space, there is a high risk of the spread of criminal behavior," the Chilean expert adds.

Several criminal groups across the region even have their roots in overcrowded prisons: Tren de Aragua in Venezuela; Los Lobos, Los Choneros and Los Tiguerones in Ecuador; and Primeiro Comando da Capital (PCC) and Comando Vermelho (CV) in Brazil.

Even when the proposal involves simply building large-scale facilities, investing in a single structure may seem attractive given the difficulties of developing public infrastructure in Latin America.

However, "there is insufficient evidence to support the claim that building mega-prisons is more cost-effective," says Renato Rivera, a senior analyst at the Global Initiative Against Transnational Organized Crime (GI-TOC).

The United Nations Standard Minimum Rules for the Treatment of Prisoners, adopted in 1955, "the recommendation has been to build medium-sized prisons housing between 1,000 and 2,000 inmates rather than mega-prisons," explains Perez Guadalupe, a professor at the Universidad del Pacifico in Lima.

"Mega-prisons, apart from being impersonal, can become extremely dangerous," says Guadalupe. As an example, the GI-TOC's Rivera highlights the widely reported prison massacres in Ecuador in 2021 that took place in the country's largest and most populated facilities.

Security, propaganda and human rights

Experts acknowledge that mass incarceration has coincided with a dramatic decline in violence in El Salvador and has strengthened the public's perception of safety. Despite reports of arbitrary arrests, abuses and more than 500 deaths in state custody in the country, announcements of new mega-prisons project an image of a strong state confronting organized crime across the region.

However, they warn that this political and symbolic impact does not guarantee sustainable results. Achieving them would require a "clear commitment" to external oversight, human rights protections and social reintegration programs, which governments have yet to demonstrate, Espinoza says.

Perez Guadalupe is particularly critical of the Salvadoran model, describing it as "pure propaganda." He believes the images released from CECOT violate human dignity. He also argues that the state must demonstrate "moral superiority over those who break the law."

Can the Salvadoran model be exported?

Although transnational organized crime represents a growing challenge across the region, the Peruvian criminologist considers El Salvador's case exceptional.

Following the mass arrests carried out under the state of emergency introduced by Bukele, the country has one of the highest incarceration rates in the world. CECOT was designed to permanently detain members of gangs such as MS-13 and Barrio 18, which are considered extremely dangerous.

However, the reality of other Latin American prison systems is different. The question is not where to lock people deprived of their liberty away forever, but rather "how we want them to leave: worse or better," Perez Guadalupe argues, pointing out that most will eventually return to society.

What are the alternatives?

In theory, the official alternative is provided by the UN Nelson Mandela Rules for the treatment of prisoners, updated in 2015. They establish principles for modern prison management, including respect for human dignity, an absolute prohibition on torture and degrading treatment and social reintegration as a central goal of imprisonment.

In practice, Latin America has developed innovative approaches in this direction. These include the APAC model in Brazil, which operates facilities without guards, weapons or violence; Conflict Prevention and Resolution Committees in Argentina; and the Alternative Criminal Justice Center in the Mexican state of Sonora.

Experts also point to the need for maximum-security prisons for specific inmate profiles, but on a smaller scale and with more precise classification of the prison population.

Finally, they emphasize that prisons, including mega-prisons, primarily address the consequences of organized crime rather than its root causes. Poverty, social exclusion and a lack of opportunities require public policies focused on employment, education and social integration to reduce the conditions that enable crime to expand in one of the world's most unequal regions.

This article was originally published in Spanish.

entries.title: APEC summit: Xi, Trump and Putin gather in Shenzhen, China
entries.summary: The presidents of China, Russia and the US have greeted each other amid the APEC summit in Shenzhen. This comes a day ahead of the trilateral talks between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Follow DW live.
entries.content:
United States of America

APEC summit: Xi, Trump and Putin gather in Shenzhen, China

Published November 17, 2026last updated November 18, 2026

The presidents of China, Russia and the US have greeted each other amid the APEC summit in Shenzhen. This comes a day ahead of the trilateral talks between Xi Jinping, Vladimir Putin and Donald Trump. Follow DW live.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • US President Donald Trump and Russian President Vladimir Putin have shaken hands for the first time in more than a year ahead of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit
  • Trump was greeted by Chinese President and summit host Xi Jinping at the airport earlier on Wednesday
  • Putin has already held talks with Xi — while trilateral talks also involving Trump are scheduled for Thursday
  • Trump is on a three-day Asia tour, having first landed in the Philippines on Tuesday

Here are the biggest headlines from Trump's Asia tour on Wednesday, November 18: 

Skip next section Sheinbaum's economy flight impresses in China

Sheinbaum's economy flight impresses in China

Mexico's Claudia Sheinbaum won praise on Chinese social media for her frugal travel plans this week, taking an economy flight to Shenzhen.

The Mexican president took a South China Airlines flight from Mexico City to Shenzhen, with posts going viral on China's Weibo social media site seemingly showing Sheinbaum chatting with other passengers on board.

She posted a short video on social media showing her being greeted by Chinese officials and schoolchildren after getting off an airport bus, as well as an earlier post showing her waiting in Mexico City's airport departures lounge.

A hashtag on Weibo about her arrival attracted more than 10 million views, with users voicing admiration for her low-cost intercontinental travel.

"It's commendable to spend taxpayer money frugally and ensure it's used where it's most needed, rather than squandering it on luxurious private jets or official travel expenses," the AFP news agency cited one user as saying.

Sheinbaum is promoting an austerity program launched by her predecessor, Andres Manuel Lopez Obrador, who put the Mexican presidential plane up for sale in 2023. 

She traveled with a large delegation of ministers to Shenzhen.

China has become particularly sensitive to the idea of corruption and wasteful public spending in recent years amid high-profile and long-running anti-corruption measures launched by President Xi Jinping, seemingly at least partly as damage-limitation efforts following a series of scandals.

Skip next section Canada's Carney, Mexico's Sheinbaum hold talks with Trump

Canada's Carney, Mexico's Sheinbaum hold talks with Trump

The leaders of Canada and Mexico have both reported on separate meetings with the US president on the sidelines of the APEC summit, amid difficult trade talks with the main economic power in the Americas. 

"The leaders discussed the work underway to reach a mutually beneficial trade agreement that would create jobs, boost affordability, and fully respect Canada's languages, culture, and sovereignty," Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney's office said. "They agreed to continue the work and to stay in close contact."

Meanwhile, Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum published a photo of her "very good meeting with President Donald Trump and his team" online, saying "we continue to make progress on our shared agenda." 

Skip next section Trump, Putin shake hands in first face-to-face encounter since Alaska summit

Trump, Putin shake hands in first face-to-face encounter since Alaska summit

The presidents of the US and Russia have shaken hands in their first in-person meeting since August 2025, when Putin was invited to Alaska for talks primarily concerning Russia's invasion of Ukraine. 

Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin shook hands in the presence of host Xi Jinping ahead of the leaders' welcome banquet at the APEC summit in Shenzhen.

The encounter follows a rare sign of progress in the US-led efforts to broker an end to the war between Russia and Ukraine, a conflict Trump repeatedly claimed he would settle in "a day" if reelected.

The two are expected to have a private meeting on Thursday.

Talks took place last week in Abu Dhabi involving Russia, Ukraine and European representatives, with Trump's negotiating team subsequently traveling to the Kremlin for a meeting with Putin and other Russian officials.

Skip next section WATCH: Xi greets Trump at the airport

WATCH: Xi greets Trump at the airport

Trump's arrival was highly choreographed: He descended from Air Force One and stood on a red carpet lined with people waving colorful pom poms. Trump and Xi hugged before shaking hands.

Skip next section Potential Trump talks touted in Shenzhen, even with Kim Jong Un

Potential Trump talks touted in Shenzhen, even with Kim Jong Un

The White House, other countries and Donald Trump himself have all listed possible or probable bilateral or multilateral talks involving the US president on the sidelines of the APEC summit in Shenzhen, beyond Thursday's highly-anticipated US-China-Russia meeting.

Some of the more notable examples are listed here:

  • Kremlin officials said they expected a meeting between just Trump and Putin, but not one long or substantial enough for fully-fledged bilateral negotiations
  • The White House said Trump would hold two separate meetings with Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney and Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum prior to the official APEC greeting ceremony
  • While in Manila, Trump himself floated the possibility of a meeting with North Korea's Kim Jong Un, but without voicing a solid intent
  • China said it had no information on a potential Trump-Kim meeting
  • Meanwhile, North Korean state media — which typically operates behind the global news cycle — has only released images of Kim visiting a ski resort and Mount Paektu, making no mention of possible Shenzhen travel plans

Skip next section Xi tells Trump China seeks 'strategically stable relationship'

Xi tells Trump China seeks 'strategically stable relationship'

Chinese news agency Xinhua has reported the first comments from Xi Jinping to Donald Trump following his arrival.

"I look forward to an in-depth exchange of views with you on major issues concerning China-US relations, Asia-Pacific cooperation, and the global landscape," Xi told Trump.

He said the talks would take place "with the aim of advancing a constructive, strategically stable relationship between our two nations — one built upon the foundations of mutual respect, fairness and reciprocity."

Despite Trump and Xi's efforts to regularly hold friendly face-to-face talks in recent months, the US and China are nevertheless embroiled in difficult trade negotiations as the two superpowers try to reconcile competing interests on various issues. 

The two sides have been periodically extending a temporary tariff truce designed to bridge the gap until they can reach a more permanent agreement, which for now has proven elusive. China announced the most recent extension earlier this month, to run until early January.

Skip next section Nvidia stops shipping US-approved chips to China

Nvidia stops shipping US-approved chips to China

The interim CEO of US chip giant Nvidia says the company is not currently shipping Hopper-generation data center products to China. 

These are some of the most advanced Nvidia products licensed for export by the US government; the company had sold such goods worth $2.4 billion (roughly €2.2 billion) in the previous quarter, Colette Kress said.

Kress replaced Jensen Huang following his resignation last week and amid the scandal over alleged Chinese attempts both to gain intelligence on the company's CEO and to circumvent import restrictions.

"Our guidance does not have any licensed Hopper data center products included, and we are no longer shipping licensed Hopper data center products to China," Kress said.

She did not specify why such deliveries had currently stopped or say whether the step would be permanent.

Huang was influential in persuading Donald Trump to allow sales of H200 Hopper processors used to train and run advanced AI models to China, reversing export controls the US had imposed in 2022 under Trump's predecessor Joe Biden.

China has called the allegations of espionage targeting Nvidia unfounded and threatened to respond in kind if restrictions on trade follow as a result of the fallout from Huang's resignation.

Skip next section Donald Trump arrives at Shenzhen Airport ahead of summit

Donald Trump arrives at Shenzhen Airport ahead of summit

US President Donald Trump has landed at Shenzhen Airport on Air Force One and disembarked. 

He left Manila in the Philippines a few hours earlier.

Trump will be attending the APEC summit but is also expected to take part in a three-way meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin and Chinese President Xi Jinping on Thursday.

Xi greeted Trump at the airport on Wednesday, mirroring a gesture Trump had recently extended during the Chinese leader's state visit to the US in September. 

Skip next section Japan's Sanae Takaichi on first China trip since becoming PM

Japan's Sanae Takaichi on first China trip since becoming PM

Sanae Takaichi arrived in China for the APEC summit, which is also her first official visit to the country as Japanese prime minister.

Takaichi's moves to bolster Japan's military and comments last year on Taiwan have upset Beijing and severely affected bilateral ties. 

In particular, Takaichi's suggestion that Tokyo could intervene militarily if Beijing sought to forcibly take Taiwan — which China considers its territory — led to friction between the regional rivals with a troubled 20th century history and ongoing territorial disputes. 

China imposed trade restrictions and urged citizens not to travel to Japan, which had become an increasingly popular tourist destination. Traffic is down by roughly half this year as a result. 

A formal one-on-one meeting between Takaichi and China's Xi Jinping is considered highly unlikely, but Japan's NHK public broadcaster did report that Xi would "personally greet her" before Wednesday's banquet.

Skip next section IN DEPTH: What Trump, Xi and Putin want

IN DEPTH: What Trump, Xi and Putin want

The leaders of China, the United States and Russia are due to hold their first trilateral meeting on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (APEC) summit this week.

Separately, US President Donald Trump will also hold talks with Chinese President Xi Jinping during the November 18-19 gathering in Shenzhen, China.

With different priorities on trade, Ukraine, Iran and arms control, what does each leader hope to gain?

Read DW's full report on what Trump, Xi and Putin are hoping to extract from the trilateral talks. 

Skip next section Canada, China taking steps to widen access for financial firms, says Carney

Canada, China taking steps to widen access for financial firms, says Carney

Canada and China are moving to give each other's financial firms greater access to their markets, Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney said during a speech at the APEC summit.

"When our businesses depend on ​too few currencies or single payment channels, disruption, when it comes, can spread quickly," ​he said, adding that China and Canada had renewed the ​currency swap arrangement ‌between their central banks and were issuing each other's currencies.

Carney's comments came a day after he and President Xi held talks in Shenzhen to produce deals to further reduce tariffs. Ottawa is re-engaging with China after years of strained relations as it looks to reduce its reliance on the US.

Skip next section Trump says US concludes 'very big trade deal' with Philippines

Trump says US concludes 'very big trade deal' with Philippines

President Trump on Wednesday said that the US has just concluded a "very big trade deal" with the Philippines, albeit without providing details. Manila has not yet confirmed any agreement.

"We've just consummated a very big trade deal, the ​biggest trade deal we've ever made so far, and it ​is a fair deal for both countries," Trump ​said during ‌a state luncheon at the Philippine presidential palace.

"We were very happy with that, and we didn't know ‌that was going to take place, but it took ‌place ​very quickly and it's a magnificent deal for both," he said.

Trade negotiations were not listed in the schedules provided by Washington or Manila.

The Philippines' ambassador to the US, Jose Manuel Romualdez ​said, "The US offered ‌for us to diversify our food supply and energy requirements."

However, Romualdez told Reuters that nothing had been signed.

Skip next section The man in the middle: Xi hosts APEC summit

The man in the middle: Xi hosts APEC summit

The two-day APEC summit has kicked off in China's southern city of Shenzhen. DW's Rik Glauert in Taipei offers a preview of what host, Xi Jinping, is hoping to achieve.

Skip next section Xi calls for 'free and open trade' as counter to US tariffs

Xi calls for 'free and open trade' as counter to US tariffs

President Xi pledged to stand against trade protectionism in his speech at the APEC summit on Wednesday, in a subtle slight towards the United States and the trade war waged by its president.

Xi urged support for what he called "free and open trade," trying to ​portray his country as a stable partner on the global stage in contrast with its main economic rival, the US, which has raised tariffs ‌under President Trump.

His remarks came after Washington announced further restrictions on China's access to advanced AI chips from companies such as Nvidia, further complicating a trade truce between the two superpowers.

Xi urged that China and Russia, together, take concrete measures to further cooperation and "lead and advance the ⁠trend toward ​a multipolar world."

Chinese and Russian news agencies reported at around noon on Wednesday that Xi and Putin had met for talks. That's the fifth time the two leaders have met this year, including once by video link.

Skip next section Putin says he expects 'big potential benefit' from meeting with China, US

Putin says he expects 'big potential benefit' from meeting with China, US

Russian President Vladimir Putin on Wednesday said he expected major benefits from his upcoming trilateral meet with US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping.

Speaking at the opening ceremony of the APEC summit, Putin called for partnership over isolation, citing a fragmented global economy and military-political risks. 

"I therefore expect big potential benefit ​from the ‌upcoming trilateral meeting between the leaders of Russia, China and ​the United ⁠States, which is scheduled to take place ⁠on ​the sidelines of the APEC summit," Putin told the summit.

The Russian leader held bilateral talks with Xi ahead of the pair's trilateral talks with Trump on Thursday.

Putin said Chinese and Russian foreign policy was working "steadily and positively on the international stage."

entries.title: How a green economy could help reverse climate change
entries.summary: Green growth promises a future in which economies thrive without destroying the environment. But is this vision realistic?
entries.content:
November 18, 2026

Green growth promises a future in which economies thrive without destroying the environment. But is this vision realistic?

Human civilization is currently profoundly unsustainable. Earth has already crossed seven of the nine planetary boundaries critical for sustaining life, including climate change, ocean acidification and biosphere integrity.

If economies and societies keep to business as usual, the Earth's vital processes will continue to be thrown wildly out of balance, threatening the future of humanity.

It's now largely accepted that if humans are to have any chance of slowing global warming and nature loss, those social and economic models must change. That's where the idea of green growth comes in.

Its promise is to keep growing the economy while reducing emissions and resource use. That involves, for instance, running factories, businesses and homes on wind, solar and other green energy instead of coal and gas, replacing gas-fired furnaces with heat pumps and  recycling and reusing resources and raw materials. 

"Basically, the idea is: business as usual, but with more sustainable technologies," said Helmut Haberl, a social ecology professor at BOKU University in Vienna. Along with his colleagues, he published a major report in 2020 evaluating more than 800 studies on green growth.

Can economies grow while emissions fall?

In principle, the world's economic output could continue to grow in the long term and generate significantly fewer emissions from the burning of fossil fuels like coal, oil and gas. That's been shown in scenarios modeled by researchers with the UN's Intergovernmental Panel on Climate Change, or IPCC.

Thanks to renewable energy and green technologies, those scenarios have already become reality in several countries and regions.

The economies of developed countries like the United Kingdom, the United States, Japan and Australia have experienced years of growth alongside sinking CO2 emissions. That's even when offshore production is included.

In the European Union, the bloc-wide economy has grown by more than 70% since 1990. Meanwhile, the EU's carbon emissions have dropped by around 40%.

But such a complete decoupling of growth and emissions is, according to Haberl and his fellow researchers, relatively rare.

In India, and in several countries in Africa and Southeast Asia, economies are becoming more efficient. But while economic performance is outpacing emissions growth, emissions are still rising in those countries and globally. This is not compatible with preventing the worst impacts of climate change.

"That doesn't mean, however, that it couldn't work in the future," said Haberl, referring to decoupling of growth and emissions.

And even though economic growth has been shown to be compatible with emissions reduction, eliminating all greenhouse gases from a polluting industry like steel or chemicals is complicated.

These sectors don't just release emissions by burning fossil fuels for energy; carbon is also a key part of the chemical processes used to create their products, notably in the steel industry. 

Replacing it with greener substitutes, or an alternative energy source like green hydrogen, requires significant investment.

Emissions aren't the only problem with economic growth

There's another hurdle: the world's high consumption of resources. A productive economy depends on many raw materials and other products: ores, chemicals, wood, cement, glass and agricultural products.

Many countries are now using green technologies to reduce the amount of resources needed to manufacture a product, for example, and are making their economies more efficient.

But that doesn't mean overall fewer resources are being used because falling costs can encourage businesses to produce more things and people to consume more. This can partially offset green savings and is called the rebound effect.

The British economy has been growing for years, emissions have been dropping and efficiency has increased, but the UK still used 7% more resources in 2023 than it did in 2001.

Global resource consumption has tripled over the last 50 years. If the world continues on the current pathway, that could increase by another 60% by 2060. It remains unclear whether green growth can deliver the emissions and resource reductions needed to stop climate change and biodiversity loss rapidly enough.

"We really need to move beyond efficiency gains in our existing production practices to look more broadly at what we consume," said Catherine Ganzleben, a sustainability and fair transitions expert at the European Environment Agency.

She told DW that people also need to reconsider how they consume and whether they really need to own everything they use in their daily life — cars, for example.

"But we can shift towards models where we share cars, so we pool our resources and have significantly lower resources per person through sharing the goods that we need."

Is degrowth the future?

Some researchers have concluded that unrestricted economic growth is no longer possible in the long term, even if it's sustainable.

Instead, they've called for degrowth. This posits slower economic growth, no growth at all or even negative growth, so that the world's ecosystems and the climate have a chance to recover and stabilize.

That applies mainly to economies in richer countries, which would need to take targeted steps to reduce their energy and resource use. Poorer countries would continue to grow until their economies and quality of life improve significantly.

Under the degrowth theory, a society's prosperity is not measured solely by the growth of its gross domestic product, but by values such as quality of life, education and community. The idea is that once countries develop to a certain point, additional growth doesn't translate into greater well-being.

Ultimately, the concept is based on the idea that human well-being and ecological sustainability is only possible in the long term with a planned, socially just reduction of material production and resource consumption. Degrowth advocates argue this would be preferable to an unplanned and potentially catastrophic economic contraction caused by escalating climate extremes.

A 2020 study by researchers from the universities of Leeds and Lausanne showed that the concept of degrowth supported the world's climate goals — and that a high quality of life didn't have to be sacrificed in exchange for a significantly lower consumption of energy and resources.

However, there is still no conclusive evidence that an entire modern economy could continue to function entirely on the degrowth principles in the long term.

Is an environmentally friendly economy possible?

Nevertheless, Haberl doesn't assume that an environmentally friendly economic model automatically goes hand in hand with sacrifice, arguing instead for a needs-based economy.

"A society isn't necessarily better off when it's producing more goods and services," he said. It all depends on how prosperity and quality of life are measured in the future, and how states decide to do business.

Today, a successful economy is measured by the growth of a country's gross domestic product — put simply, the worth of all of its goods and services. This calculation doesn't account for income distribution, unpaid work, quality of life or environmental damage.

"The highest possible real incomes for every individual would probably not be compatible with ecological goals in the long term," said Haberl. "On the other hand, an increase in prosperity — related to a higher quality of life — would be."

An analysis by the European Environment Agency (EEA) pointed out that the idea of steady growth is part of the world's economic cycle, and deeply anchored in our institutions, norms and societal discourse. The job market and tax system are also closely tied to gross domestic product growth. A shrinking economy would therefore require a fundamental shift in our way of thinking.

Countries face a dilemma: a steadily growing economy is not compatible with ecological goals, according to the EEA. On the other side, a sharp decline in growth could trigger enormous social upheaval.

And the correlation is much more complex than the idea of "less is more," as highlighted by an EEA study in November 2021. "The fact that GDP growth has been harmful for the environment does not necessarily mean that declining GDP would be good for the environment," noted the report.

Achieving green growth while respecting environmental limits would require an "unprecedented decoupling of economic activity from environmental and climate pressures. Whether this is feasible is currently uncertain."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Germany news: Merz's coalition agrees on electricity tax cut
entries.summary: The coalition government has agreed on an electricity tax cut for households amid energy shocks from the war in Iran. Meanwhile, the BSW party has failed to push for a recount of the 2025 election. DW has more.
entries.content:
Published November 18, 2026last updated November 18, 2026

The coalition government has agreed on an electricity tax cut for households amid energy shocks from the war in Iran. Meanwhile, the BSW party has failed to push for a recount of the 2025 election. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD) have agreed on a tax cut for households and businesses for 2027
  • A previous cut only applied to industry, agriculture and forestry
  • A top court has rejected a recount appeal by the BSW party over the 2025 election

Here is a roundup of the top news stories from and about Germany on Wednesday, November 18, 2026:

Skip next section WATCH — How the German far right is split over immigration

WATCH — How the German far right is split over immigration

The Republicans' losses in the US midterm elections have exposed a feud within the far right in Germany.

A rare public disagreement between Alternative for Germany (AfD) leaders over immigration reveals who is winning the battle for the party's future.

Watch below for more on the rift among AfD politicians.

Skip next section Governing coalition agrees to electricity tax cut

Governing coalition agrees to electricity tax cut

Germany's governing coalition has agreed to reduce electricity tax for households and businesses.

The cut will lower the electricity tax rate for 2027 to the European minimum level.

The agreement between Chancelor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU/CSU and his junior coalition partner, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), was reached after multiple failed attempts.

Funding for the tax cut has only been secured for the year 2027, but the coalition stressed in a summary document of the agreement that it aimed to achieve a "permanent reduction." An extension is contingent on finding a way to fund it into 2028, according to the paper.

The coalition partners said that the tax cut will be funded by surplus funds from subsidies under the renewable energy bill, as the government anticipates lower demand for renewable energy subsidies next year.

The government is also to introduce a three-month cap on fuel prices in January.

The CDU/CSU and SPD promised in their 2025 coalition deal to cut taxes for all consumers, but initially only applied a reduction for industry, agriculture and forestry. Wednesday's agreement extends cuts to households and to businesses that did not qualify for the initial reduction.

Germany has some of the highest electricity prices in Europe, in part thanks to shocks following Russia's 2022 invasion of Ukraine and by the United States and Israel's war with Iran.

The Wednesday agreement still needs to be incorporated into the 2027 budget. The budget must then be cleared by the parliamentary budget committee, with the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag, expected to give final approval on November 27.

The 2027 federal budget proposal marks a major shift in German fiscal policy, with Berlin taking on increasing debt, citing the need to finance repairs to the country's crumbling infrastructure, carry out the energy transition and expand and modernize the military.

Skip next section Spike in holiday requests ahead of GTA6 launch

Spike in holiday requests ahead of GTA6 launch

Germans are seemingly requesting days off work to play GTA 6 ahead of the videogame's Thursday release, according to data from the HR software company Personio.

GTA 6 is part of the popular open-world, action-adventure series "Grand Theft Auto," in which the player can explore a city, commit crimes outside, and complete hours worth of missions.

The latest installment has been eagerly awaited by gamers for 13 years, having been subject to two delays and multiple leaks.

The Munich-based personnel software provider Personio said that Germany saw 38% more requests for days off than usual for the launch of GTA 6, and a 58% in requests for compensatory time off for overtime hours worked.

However, economists do not expect the rush to play the long-awaited game to have any impact on the German economy.

"The economy won't collapse because of GTA, just because some people decide to take a bit of time off," media economist Jörg Müller-Lietzkow was cited by ZDF as saying.

Skip next section Net household incomes rising, but inequality remains — report

Net household incomes rising, but inequality remains — report

Real net household incomes in Germany are rising again following a period of high inflation, according to a report from the German economics research institute DIW Berlin.

The report revealed that overall income satisfaction has risen significantly as more and more people in Germany are managing to save.

However, the rise has not yet offset earlier losses from high inflation rates in 2022 and 2023, the institute said.

Incomes have grown by an average of nearly one-third since 1995, but inequality has risen significantly — while top incomes have risen by over 50%, those in the middle of the curve have risen by around a quarter and those at the lower end have largely remained stagnant.

DIW Berlin warned that the long-term risk of falling into poverty has risen to 17%.

However, the report's author stressed that the increase in inequality was due to a shift over a longer period and it had not significantly widened in recent years.

"While income inequality in Germany has risen over the long term, it has remained largely stable in recent years," DIW Berlin researcher Markus Grabka said.

Skip next section Merz briefly left electricity tax cut talks out of irritation — report

Merz briefly left electricity tax cut talks out of irritation — report

German Chancellor Friedrich Merz left Tuesday night's coalition talks on an electricity tax cut out of frustration, German tabloid newspaper Bild reported on Wednesday.

Bild cited participants of the coalition meeting as saying that Merz left the talks in Berlin around midnight local time (2300 UTC) over demands made by his CDU/CSU conservative bloc's junior coalition partners, the center-left Social Democrats (SPD).

Before leaving, Merz said "I'm not putting up with this anymore," according to Bild. He later returned to talks, reportedly after speaking to Markus Söder, who leads the Christian Social Union (CSU), the Bavarian sister party to Merz's own Christian Democrats (CDU).

The coalition ultimately agreed upon a reduction in the electricity tax for households and businesses, bringing the rate for 2027 to the European minimum level.

According to Bild, the SPD had insisted on guaranteeing funding for the measure well beyond 2027.

The tax cut is to be funded by surplus funds from subsidies under the renewable energy bill and its extension is contingent on finding a way to fund it into 2028, according to a summary paper of an agreement reached between the two coalition factions.

Bild cited sources close to Merz as saying that the talks had been very difficult and intricate, with the CDU arguing that the issue could have been resolved within an hour, rather than extending deep into the night.

The two parties have regularly been at odds over key policy questions, particularly around budget and taxation issues.

Skip next section Live lobster found on Munich train

Live lobster found on Munich train

Police were called to the lost and found for Munich's S-Bahn suburban rail network after a live lobster was found on one of the trains.

The lobster, weighing some 3 kilograms (around 6.6 pounds), was found in a Styrofoam box by S-Bahn workers on Tuesday morning.

He was initially treated with a saline solution and given the nickname "Günni."

Police determined that the crustacean had initially been purchased from a wholesale market for hospitality and retail in Munich and escorted it back to the point of sale.

Skip next section Foreign Minister Wadephul visits Armenia, Azerbaijan

Foreign Minister Wadephul visits Armenia, Azerbaijan

German Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul is visiting Armenia and Azerbaijan on Wednesday.

He is set to make his way to Yerevan, Armenia after his visit to the Azerbaijani capital, Baku.

Discussions were to focus on implementing a joint strategic agenda signed by German Chancellor Friedrich Merz and Azerbaijan's President Ilham Aliyev in July, according to the ministry.

The leaders were also to discuss the supply of natural gas and crude oil from Azerbaijan.

They were also to touch on the peace process between Armenia and Azerbaijan, which fought wars over the Nagorno-Karabakh territory in 2020 and 2023.

Germany supports 'positive momentum' in Armenia-Azerbaijan peace

The ministry cited Wadephul as saying Berlin aimed to capitalize on the "positive momentum" between Baku and Yerevan that had developed since the 2025 peace summit in Washington.

Wadephul said that he also aims to examine Russia's influence in the southern Caucasus.

"In the South Caucasus too, we are seeing Russia try to retain its influence — at the expense of the people and their future," the minister said on Tuesday before embarking on a flight to the region.

Armenia and Azerbaijan were part of the former Soviet Union and Russia maintains significant influence in the region.

Skip next section Constitutional Court rejects BSW request for 2025 vote recount

Constitutional Court rejects BSW request for 2025 vote recount

Germany's Constitutional Court has rejected an appeal brought by the populist Alliance for Social Justice and Economic Reason (BSW) against the February 2025 federal election result, dashing the party's hopes it could trigger a recount that would allow it to enter parliament.

The BSW party, formerly known as the Sahra Wagenknecht Alliance after the name of its founder, narrowly failed to reach the 5% threshold to enter the lower house of parliament, the Bundestag.

Having received 4,981% of the vote, it would have needed just 9,529 more votes to enter the chamber.

The BSW maintained that there had been an error in the vote count and that the party could be assigned some 35 seats.

If the party were to enter parliament, a rearrangement of seats could also threaten the majority held by the current ruling coalition made up of Chancellor Friedrich Merz's conservative CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left Social Democrats.

Lack of recount 'slap in the face of democracy' — BSW

"Everything points to the conclusion that Merz is an illegitimate chancellor and that the current Bundestag is not composed in accordance with the constitution," party founder Sahra Wagenknecht told Germany's DPA news agency before the court published its ruling.

"Without access to the actual ballots, it is impossible to provide further evidence or indications of counting errors to the detriment of the BSW."

She said that if the court were to rule against the party's appeal, this would be a "slap in the face of democracy."

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Guten Tag from the DW newsroom in Bonn!

Germany's coalition government, made up of the conservative CDU/CSU alliance and the center-left Social Democrats (SPD), has agreed to an electricity tax cut.

Germany's Constitutional Court has rejected an appeal by the populist BSW party to do a recount of the 2025 election after they failed to top the 5% hurdle to enter the Bundestag.
